concept.title: Lift hardcoded game balance numbers into editable spreadsheets
concept.text: Pulls every hardcoded enemy stat, item price, drop rate and spawn rule out of a game mod's scripts into a spreadsheet with source locations, so designers can tune balance in one place.
concept.pitch: For modders and small game teams whose balance lives as magic numbers scattered across hundreds of script files, so designers can't see or compare it. The tool turns the code into a flat table (entity, field, value, unit guess, file:line) and can write edits back to the exact locations. Designers have spreadsheets and the data is in code, and nobody has done the one-off lift because it is too tedious by hand.

closest.what: Non-AI tool (2021) that parses balance values from Chivalry: Medieval Warfare vanilla/mod source files into a spreadsheet; only dumps a weapon stamina-drain matrix, no write-back, no file:line table.

Node CLI that parses balance values out of Chivalry: Medieval Warfare vanilla/mod source files into a spreadsheet. It only dumps one weapon stamina-drain matrix, is game-specific, and has no write-back. Last pushed 2021, 0 stars.

'gamenumerics' MCP server (seen in WebSearch results, page not opened) letting a coding agent import xlsx game config tables, audit growth curves and run simulations; works on existing tables, does not lift hardcoded numbers out of code.
KSP mod that dumps part and module values to CSV for balancing; export only, reads runtime data rather than scripts, no write-back, no AI.

concept.title: Resurrect an orphaned booking app's dead server
concept.text: Captures traffic between a salon's orphaned booking client and its dead vendor server, infers the message formats, and reimplements a drop-in server so the paid software keeps syncing appointments on current Windows.
concept.pitch: For businesses that bought a licensed desktop and phone booking system, then watched the vendor shut down its cloud, leaving the software unusable. The owner's own client runs against a local replacement server, rebuilt from recorded traffic, local certificates and the client's binary. It restores something the owner already paid for. It has not been done because the work is unglamorous and the vendors are gone, so there is no one to ask.

closest.what: wire-pod: community-built replacement server for the Anki/DDL Vector robot after the vendor's cloud went down; lets owners' existing devices keep working against a local server. Same method and outcome, consumer robot not business software, hand-built.
TeddyCloud: open-source server replacement for the Boxine cloud used by the Toniebox, built by reverse engineering the device protocol.
HN comment: author reverse engineered the OUYA API after its servers shut down in 2019 and built a documented re-implementation so consoles work again.
Python server emulator for a mobile game, built by reverse engineering the client API for preservation. No AI mentioned, and it is a game rather than business software.

concept.title: Detect silent wearable firmware changes that threaten studies
concept.text: Diffs successive firmware images and companion-app packages of a fitness wearable, flags changed step, sleep and heart-rate algorithms, and writes a dated data-validity memo for research teams whose cohort data spans those versions.
concept.pitch: For research groups and graduate students who collect activity data on consumer wearables and cannot tell when a vendor update quietly changed the metric. It unpacks two or more versions of a device's firmware and companion app, locates the signal-processing code that changed, and reports which date ranges in a dataset are not comparable. Nobody does this because scientists treat the device as a black box and hackers have no research customer.

closest.what: Collins et al. 2019 Sensors, 'Version Reporting and Assessment Approaches for New and Updated Activity and Heart Rate Monitors'. It documents the exact problem: firmware and software updates change device performance, same-model devices on different versions are distinct, and Garmin Vivosmart HR had 14 versions in ~30 months. Its remedy is an empirical bench and treadmill re-validation protocol plus version reporting. It does no firmware diffing and has no tooling.

Paper 'Not all steps are equal: Changing algorithms in wearable trackers changes outcomes'. Documents the problem: vendors change tracker algorithms mid-study, and the paper warns researchers to watch for it. It gives no tool that diffs firmware or apps, and no memo.

2024 commentary on research-grade devices. Notes that firmware can change how sensor output becomes counts, cites the 2021 Apple HRV change, and says Oura lets researchers freeze firmware. It names the problem and mitigations, but no diffing method.

News coverage of Apple Watch HRV exports differing between 2020 and 2021 because OS updates changed the algorithms, with Beiwe's developer (Harvard) concerned. It shows the pain point and that researchers detect it by re-exporting data and comparing. No detection tool is mentioned.

concept.title: Neighbors' lease clauses compared side by side
concept.text: Compares redacted leases that tenants of one landlord voluntarily upload, aligns clauses across copies, and publishes a shared map showing which fees and terms differ between neighbors for the same unit type.
concept.pitch: For tenant associations and building groups where each renter signed a nominally identical lease and none can tell whether they got the same terms. Members upload their own redacted lease, the system aligns clause by clause, and the group sees a diff map: this late fee is 5 percent for most units and 10 percent for yours, this renewal clause appears in only seven leases. Individuals only ever see their own copy, so the comparison, which needs many contracts at once, has been out of reach.

closest.what: Harvey: upload many leases and summarize or compare key terms across the set. Same cross-lease clause alignment, but built for legal teams and portfolios, not pooled tenant uploads.

Leases as Forms (academic): analysis of ~170,000 Philadelphia eviction-court leases; finds leases vary more between landlords than within them and flags unlawful terms. Court-record data, not tenant-contributed, no per-group diff map, not shown to use an AI assistant. Seen in search results only (publisher page redirected on fetch).

LeaseCheck: renters anonymously report rent, fees, landlords and safety; compiled into transparency reports. Crowdsourced and tenant-side, but structured reports, not clause-aligned lease uploads. Landing page only, scale unverified.
DenserAI: landlord and property-manager tool that compares lease terms across properties. Mechanism matches; audience is the landlord.

concept.title: Release notes versus firmware binaries across five years
concept.text: Downloads every public firmware release of a consumer gadget line, unpacks and diffs them, and tabulates what silently changed in endpoints, permissions, ciphers and features against what the release notes claimed.
concept.pitch: For privacy researchers, consumer journalists and owners deciding whether to update. It treats a product's update history as a dataset and asks what the vendor changed that it never said. Nobody does this at scale because unpacking, diffing and reading dozens of images per product is weeks of grind.

closest.what: Public, continuously updated Apple IPSW firmware diffs across many iOS/iPadOS/macOS releases (via the ipsw tool). It is the same method (unpack and diff every release) but is aimed at security researchers, covers Apple only, and does no comparison against release notes or any privacy tabulation.

AI-written reports built on ipsw diffing of iOS releases. It uses AI to describe what changed between firmware builds, but is vulnerability-oriented, covers a single platform, and does not compare against release-note claims.

Fetches old and new binaries, runs Ghidriff diffs, then an LLM pipeline (OpenAI, Claude or Ollama) writes severity-rated reports. This is AI-assisted binary diffing, but for security patch diffing. It has no release-notes comparison, no multi-year corpus and no consumer-gadget focus.

Pre-alpha multi-agent LLM pipeline. Ghidra decompiles two binaries, an analyzer classes each change as bugfix, feature, refactor or security tweak, and a critic and clusterer follow. The only example is a cJSON library version pair, and it does not check release notes.

concept.title: Reconcile relatives' conflicting memories into one family recipe
concept.text: Interviews each relative separately about a grandmother's signature dish, then has a mediator agent reconcile their conflicting memories into one recipe card that marks disputed steps and lists a cook-off test plan.
concept.pitch: For families trying to save a dish nobody wrote down. Each relative talks to their own interviewer agent by phone voice note or text, and a mediator compares the versions, finds where they agree, and turns the disagreements (lard or butter, how long to rest the dough) into a small cook-off test. Nobody has done it because it needs one agent per witness plus a reconciler, and the people who cook for family don't usually think of multi-agent setups.

closest.what: Human practice guide for reconstructing a lost family recipe: oral histories from several relatives, ranges, repeated test attempts, reaching agreement on a version. Same outcome done manually, no AI or tool (seen in search snippet, not opened).

Voice-recording AI archiver that transcribes relatives' recipe stories into structured recipe cards (opened README). Single-narrator capture; no multi-witness comparison, dispute marking or cook-off plan.

Heirloom AI (open source, Gemini): turns recipe cards, voice recordings and cooking videos into structured recipe entries with confidence levels and 'speculative gaps' for family to verify. No multi-relative interviews, no reconciliation of conflicting versions, no cook-off plan.

Achiote (npm / KyaniteLabs MCP server, for Claude Code and Codex): reconstructs a family food memory into structured clues, a research plan and a minimum-viable nostalgia cue, and suggests follow-up questions for relatives. Works from one person's memory; no per-relative interviewer agents, no reconciling of conflicting accounts, no test plan.
